Hi Aditya —

Thanks for the call earlier — quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so your team can scope a realistic PoC. Great to meet you and Marissa.

Summary of our targets/constraints:
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT): target <= 150ms P90 for short prompts (<= 64 tokens).
- Sustained throughput: 200 requests/sec across region (est. 3 AZs) during peak.
- Concurrency: typical burst to 50 concurrent real-time sessions; baseline ~20 concurrent.
- Streaming: customer-facing responses must stream back as they are generated. We prefer SSE for browser clients but can support WebSocket if required.
- Chunk cadence: ideally chunks every ~200ms for medium responses (~200-400 tokens); larger responses can be burstier.

Attached is our internal latency report and a sample of payload sizes.

Questions for qualification:
1) Can Redwood meet TTFT P90 <= 150ms for prompts in the 16–64 token range with streaming enabled?
2) If so, on which deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and what configuration (GPU type, batching, cache settings) do you recommend?
3) How does streaming method choice (SSE vs WebSocket) affect TTFT and chunk cadence?
4) What kind of baseline benchmarks / artifacts can you share before a PoC?

Next steps we’d like: a short written plan and a proposed technical deep-dive with your engineering team. We can make time tomorrow or Wednesday afternoon PT.

Thanks —
Julia
Senior Product Manager
StreamChat Inc.

Attachments:
- streamchat-latency-report.pdf (3 pages)
- sample-payloads.json (list of typical prompts and sizes)

Julia —

Thanks for the clear summary and the attachments — very helpful. Short answers up front, then a proposed plan.

Short answers:
1) TTFT P90 <= 150ms for 16–64 token prompts: yes, achievable, with caveats (see below).
2) Deployment & config: Dedicated GPUs with optimized kernels + our continuous batching disabled for low-latency streams is the typical path. For your scale I'd recommend a Dedicated pool on A100s (or H100 if you need headroom) with KV prefix caching and 1–2 response-streaming workers per pod. Hosted can hit similar numbers but requires reservation (Dedicated gives more predictable SLAs).
3) SSE vs WebSocket: both supported. WebSocket adds minimal handshake overhead and is slightly better for low-latency two-way flows; SSE is simpler for browsers. The biggest TTFT drivers are model latency, GPU warm/cold state, and initial scheduling — not the transport.
4) Baseline artifacts: we can share internal microbenchmarks (ttft p50/p90/p99 for model variants), a short playback of streaming chunk cadence, and a sample PoC test plan.

Caveats / details:
- TTFT components: request ingress/network + routing ~20–40ms (typical), model kernel exec ~30–80ms depending on size & quantization, SDK + HTTP stack ~10–20ms. These stack up; 150ms P90 is realistic with the configuration above for short prompts.
- Batching: we typically disable cross-request batching for strict TTFT SLOs and instead rely on KV caching + small per-request micro-batching when helpful.
- Chunk cadence: we can control chunk flush frequency; 150–250ms cadence for ~200-token responses is standard on Dedicated. We provide tuning knobs for cadence vs per-token cost.

Proposed next steps:
1) Technical deep dive (45m) with your infra/eng + our serving engineers — propose 2028-03-21 10:00am PT.
2) Provide a short bench packet (expected ttft numbers and streaming sample) by EOD 2028-03-20.
3) Run a scoped PoC: 1-week smoke test on a Dedicated pool with your sample payloads + a perf script we’ll supply.

I’ve attached a short PoC checklist and a PDF with high-level TTFT tradeoffs. Marissa, Neha — please join the deep dive; Neha can own the PoC setup.

Attaching: redwood-ttft-sla.pdf, PoC-setup-instructions.docx

—
